paper_title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

Introduction Looped transformers have attracted attention for combining strong performance with efficient use of parameters and training memory. By repeatedly applying shared block of layers, they increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025). To reduce the cost of training these repeated blocks, several looped language models use truncated backpropagation through time (BPTT), propagating gradients only through the final loops while executing the earlier loops without tracking gradients (Geiping et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026b; McLeish et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Truncation introduces new tradeoff: it saves backward computation and activation memory during training but can weaken the gains from looping (Schwethelm et al., 2026). To achieve the best performance under fixed training compute budget, we must therefore decide how to divide compute among forward loops, backward loops, model size, and training tokens. Existing scaling studies examine prescribed backpropagation recipes rather than jointly modeling forward and backward loop counts. Schwethelm et al. (2026) compare full BPTT with truncation to half the loops, fitting separate scaling law to each recipe. Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) varies backward-loop counts in small-model experiments but fixes them to half the forward-loop count in its scaling study, leaving their joint optimization to future work. These studies characterize specific recipes but do not provide unified law for choosing both loop counts across model sizes and token budgets  (Table 1)  . We thus ask the following question: How do model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loops jointly affect loss, and should we truncate backpropagation under fixed training compute budget? To characterize how these quantities affect loss, we conduct nearly 600 training runs, including scaling suite spanning 58M919M non-embedding parameters, over three orders of magnitude in training tokens per parameter, and up to 16 forward loops. We independently vary forward and backward loop counts across model sizes and token budgets and fit unified scaling law. The scaling law expresses the benefit of looping through an effective parameter countthe size of non-looped model that achieves the same loss at the same token budget. Fully trained loops increase the effective parameter count with diminishing returns, while truncation discounts this gain. We then use the scaling law to decide whether to truncate, and the answer depends on whether the forward-loop count is prescribed. When it is, the law recovers the benefit of truncation reported in prior work (Schwethelm et al., 2026): the saved backward compute supports larger model and more training tokens, which more than offset the discounted loop gain. When both loop counts can be chosen, however, the law favors full BPTT. Reducing the forward-loop count frees compute for additional backward loops until every remaining loop is trained, and under the fitted law this reallocation yields more effective parameters at the same compute than the original truncated setting. Separately fitted laws and matched-compute experiments support this advantage (5). Building on this preference for full BPTT, we additionally study how to allocate compute among loop count, training tokens, and model size. Consider first setting where model size is predetermined, for example due to device memory constraints. At fixed model size, increasing the loop count is an effective way to increase the effective parameter count; however, additional loops offer diminishing gains while increasing the cost per token. The law precisely characterizes the optimal tradeoff between loop count and training tokens, allocating most additional compute to tokens and increasing the loop count only slowly. This result extends Parcaes fixed-size allocation analysis (Prairie et al., 2026) beyond prescribed truncation rule. When model size is also free, compute can instead support more unique parameters; under our leading-FLOP approximation, the law favors Truncate or Not? With little more training compute, such smaller model surpasses the compute-optimal non-looped model (6). Our contributions are threefold: unified scaling law based on effective parameters. We develop and validate law that expresses loop gains and truncation discounts through an effective parameter count, jointly modeling model size, training tokens, and independent forward and backward loop counts (4). An explanation of when truncation pays. We show why truncation can pay at prescribed forward-loop count and why joint forwardbackward allocation favors full BPTT under the fitted law, supported by matched-compute experiments (5). Compute-allocation rules and parameter-efficient training. We derive allocation rules for fixed and free model size and demonstrate that two fully trained loops nearly match computeoptimal non-looped models while having substantially fewer trainable parameters (6). Figure 1 previews the three results: loops add effective parameters and truncation discounts them; at fixed model size the best loop count grows with compute; two fully trained loops match the loss of non-looped model with fewer parameters for little more compute. Related work Looped transformers Depth-wise parameter sharing in Universal Transformers and ALBERT decouples computational depth from the number of trainable parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019). Theoretical and controlled studies show how recurrence supports iterative programs, in-context learning algorithms, and depth-sensitive reasoning (Giannou et al., 2023; Saunshi et al., Truncate or Not? 2025; Yang et al., 2024). In language model pretraining, Huginn uses preluderecurrentcoda architecture (Geiping et al., 2025), while Ouro scales looped pretraining to 7.7T tokens (Zhu et al., 2025). Other work adds recurrence to pretrained models (Bae et al., 2025a; McLeish et al., 2025) or adapts depth at inference (Bae et al., 2025b; Jeddi et al., 2026). Recent architectures improve recurrence through residual and hyper-connections (Fu et al., 2026; Marchenko et al., 2026; Prairie et al., 2026; Zeitoun et al., 2026) or MoE routing (Chen et al., 2026a; Csordás et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). These studies show that looping improves parameter efficiency across architectures; we instead fix the architecture and ask how to train its loops and allocate compute. Training through recurrent depth Truncated BPTT limits gradient propagation to subset of recurrent steps, saving activation memory and backward compute at the cost of biased gradients (Tallec and Ollivier, 2017; Williams and Peng, 1990). It is the common recipe for looped language models, which backpropagate through the last few loops or half of them (Geiping et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026), and recursive reasoning models often keep only the last step (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Wang et al., 2025). surveys these recipes in more detail. Implicit models likewise differentiate only few steps at the fixed point (Bai et al., 2019; Geng et al., 2021b), and truncated BPTT in looped transformers can be read as truncated Neumann series of the fixed-point gradient (Huang et al., 2026b; Movahedi et al., 2026). The few studies that measure what truncation costs compare training recipes at fixed forward depth (Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad, 2026; Huang et al., 2026a; Ren and Liu, 2026; Salvatori et al., 2026). We instead vary the backward depth independently of the forward depth, weighing the compute that truncation saves against the loop gain it costs. Scaling laws for recurrence Sizedata scaling laws quantify how parameters and training tokens jointly determine loss (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020; Videau et al., 2026). For looped models, some laws fit each architecture separately (Chen et al., 2026c; Lee et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), while others model the loop count explicitly  (Table 1)  through additive loss terms (Zhu et al., 2025) or effective parameters with linear, power-law, or bounded gains (Chen et al., 2026b; Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026). Closest to our work, Iso-Depth (Schwethelm et al., 2026) fits separate laws for full and half-length backpropagation and finds that truncation weakens the loop gain but lowers the loss at fixed forward-loop count by freeing compute, while Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) finds at fixed model size that loops and tokens should grow together with compute but ties the backward loops to half the forward loops and leaves their joint choice open. Our law instead treats the backward-loop count as separate variable, combining coupled sizedata scaling (Videau et al., 2026) with bounded loop gains (Chen et al., 2026b). It recovers the truncation benefit at prescribed forward-loop count but favors full BPTT when both counts are free (5). Looped MoE models commonly use two loops (Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). For dense models, our law ranks two fully trained loops first among looped settings, since they provide nearly the effective size of two untied copies (6.2), and in our runs they nearly match compute-optimal models without looping with substantially fewer non-embedding parameters (6.3). Conclusion Truncated BPTT saves compute, but whether it lowers the loss depends on which quantities are held fixed. We fit scaling law that expresses every loop setting as effective parameters, with gain that saturates and shrinks under truncation (4). Under this law, truncation helps only when 2Including the optimizer update, as in Table 11; the forward and backward passes alone take 2.0 1019 FLOPs. Truncate or Not? the forward-loop count is prescribed. When both loop counts are chosen, full BPTT is optimal at every model size and compute we analyze (5). The law also determines how to allocate compute. At fixed model size, most additional compute should go to data, and the number of fully trained loops grows only as about C0.24 (6.1). When model size is free, the law favors no looping, but two fully trained loops come close: with 2732% fewer non-embedding parameters they nearly match the compute-optimal non-looped model at equal compute, and with 27% fewer parameters they achieve lower loss at 8% more compute (6.3). Limitations Our main limitation is the focus on dense models: we do not study mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, so whether our conclusions on truncation and compute allocation extend to looped MoE models remains open. Second, we measure validation loss only and do not establish whether the observed gains translate to downstream task performance or reasoning ability. Third, our experiments are capped at 16, so the gain ceiling and later switches to more loops remain extrapolations. Related scaling sweeps reach eight loops in Schwethelm et al. (2026) and mean training loop counts of twelve in Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026). Much deeper recurrence can exacerbate training instability, including residual explosion and loss spikes (Fu et al., 2026; Prairie et al., 2026); developing stable training recipes for that regime is beyond our scope. Finally, we fix the ratio of non-embedding parameters in the combined prelude and coda to those in the recurrent block for each model size. Varying this ratio to study how parameter allocation affects the gains from looping and the compute-optimal loop counts is direction for future work. Extended related work Training through recurrent depth Truncated BPTT limits gradient propagation to subset of recurrent steps, saving activation memory and backward compute at the cost of biased gradients (Tallec and Ollivier, 2017; Williams and Peng, 1990). Looped language models often supervise the final output and backpropagate through only the last few loops. Huginn and retrofitted models use at most eight backward steps (Geiping et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025), Parcae and IsoDepth backpropagate through half of the loops (Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026), URM runs the first loops without gradients (Gao et al., 2025), and looped MoE models supervise within recurrent segments (He et al., 2026). The same truncation trains looped models converted from pretrained language models (Park et al., 2026), recurrent-depth models for robot control and dynamics forecasting (Lai et al., 2026; Tur et al., 2026), and looped refinement in diffusion language models (Sun et al., 2026). Recursive reasoning models use even shorter backward horizons. Hierarchical recurrent models backpropagate through only the final steps (Han, 2026; Wang et al., 2025, 2026a), and TRM and its successors run all but the last recursion without gradients (Asadulaev et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2026; Freinschlag et al., 2026; Hakimi, 2026; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Nejati Manzari et al., 2026; Salvatori et al., 2026; Sghaier et al., 2026). For algorithmic extrapolation, recurrent networks and looped transformers run random number of iterations without gradients before the supervised ones, or compute the loss over window of the last loops (Bansal et al., 2022; Labovich, 2026; Yang et al., 2024). Implicit models replace backpropagation through the solver with implicit differentiation (Bai et al., 2019) or with one-step, Jacobian-free, and phantom gradients that differentiate only few steps at the fixed point (Geng et al., 2021a,b; Wu Fung et al., 2022). Such approximations train implicit models for optical flow, diffusion, and language modeling (Bai et al., 2022; Bai and Melas-Kyriazi, 2024; Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad, 2026; Pokle et al., 2022; Schöne et al., 2025), and truncated BPTT in looped transformers can be read as truncated Neumann series of the fixed-point gradient (Huang et al., 2026b; Movahedi et al., 2026). Few studies measure what truncation costs. Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad (2026) find that the one-step gradient nearly matches the perplexity of the exact implicit gradient at fraction of its memory, Huang et al. (2026a) find that truncation lowers or raises Sudoku accuracy depending on the latent structure, Salvatori et al. (2026) find that the required gradient window grows with the propagation distance of the graph, and Ren and Liu (2026) argue that the one-step gradient delays the stabilization of hierarchical reasoning models. These studies compare training recipes at fixed forward depth; we vary the backward depth independently of the forward depth, weighing the compute that truncation saves against the loop gain it costs. Scaling laws for recurrence Sizedata scaling laws quantify how parameters and training tokens jointly determine loss (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Kaplan et al., 2020; Videau et al., 2026), and their compute-optimal predictions depend on how the laws are fitted and compute is counted (Besiroglu et al., 2024; Choshen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Pearce and Song, 2024; Porian et al., 2024). Extensions account for architectural choices such as MoE sparsity (Abnar et al., 2025; Clark et al., 2022; Krajewski et al., 2024). For looped models, some laws fit each architecture separately (Chen et al., 2026c; Lee et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), while others model the loop count explicitly  (Table 1)  through additive loss terms (Zhu et al., 2025) or effective parameters with linear, power-law, or bounded gains (Chen et al., 2026b; Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026). Among these scaling-law studies of looped transformers, Iso-Depth (Schwethelm et al., 2026) and Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) are particularly related to our work. Iso-Depth fits separate laws for full and half-length backpropagation and finds that truncation weakens the loop gain but lowers the loss at fixed forward-loop count by freeing compute. At fixed model size, Parcae finds that loops and tokens should grow together with compute, but ties the backward loops to half the forward loops and leaves Truncate or Not? their joint choice open. Our law instead treats the backward-loop count as separate variable, combining coupled sizedata scaling (Videau et al., 2026) with bounded loop gains (Chen et al., 2026b). It recovers the truncation benefit at prescribed forward-loop count but favors full BPTT when both counts are free (5). In looped MoE models, two loops are the common choice (He et al., 2026): SMELT finds them better than three or four under matched budgets (Wang et al., 2026b), and Loopie finds the marginal benefit of recurrence largest at two (Gao et al., 2026). For dense models, our law ranks two fully trained loops first among looped settings, since they provide nearly the effective size of two untied copies of the block while further loops add less (6.2). In our runs, two-loop models nearly match compute-optimal models without looping at equal compute while having substantially fewer non-embedding parameters (6.3).

In training step (Figure 3a), the prelude maps the tokens to s0, every loop reads s0 again through the input injection, and the state sT entering the last loops is treated as constant. The gradient therefore reaches the coda, the last loops and, through the injection, the prelude; the first loops run forward only, and evaluation 1 ], the ℓr pre-norm transformer runs all loops. Each loop (Figure 3b) applies Winj to [ s0 ; st layers of and an RMSNorm, with the same weights in every loop. At 2 FLOPs per parameter and token for forward pass and 4 for backward pass (Figure 3c), the prelude and coda cost 6, each forward loop 2 and each backward loop 4 more, giving 6Nonce + (2T + 4B)Nrec = 6Ncomp FLOPs per token (5.1), before attention and output (D.1); the optimizer adds cost per step (D.3). Full and truncated backpropagation through the loops This appendix writes out the gradients that full and truncated BPTT compute for the recurrence of (3.1), and the fixed-point argument that motivates truncation (3). The truncated gradient loop setting (T, B) executes forward loops and backpropagates through only the last B: the state sT is detached from the computation graph, so the first loops run without gradients. To make this precise, we denote for loop of (3.1) the Jacobian with respect to the incoming state and the derivative with respect to θ with the incoming state fixed by Jt = Φθ(st st 1; s0) , θΦt = Φθ(st θ 1; s0) . The loss depends on θ only through sT , so θL = (L/sT ) (dsT /dθ), and it suffices to compare dsT /dθ under full and truncated BPTT. The chain rule sums one contribution per loop, and detaching sT keeps only the last B, giving the truncated gradient gB: dsT dθ = t= JT Jt+1 θΦt, gB = t=T B+1 JT Jt+1 θΦt, (B.1) where the empty product for = is the identity. Truncation keeps the contributions with the fewest Jacobian products and drops the rest. The prelude gradient is truncated in the same way. Truncation from fixed point view Whether the dropped contributions matter depends on the loop dynamics, and the deep-equilibrium view (Bai et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025) gives an idealized answer. Suppose the loops approach fixed point = Φθ(s; s0), so that Jt and θΦt θΦ for the loops that carry gradient. If the spectral radius of is below one, the implicit function Truncate or Not? theorem gives the gradient of the fixed point, and Neumann series expands it into the same per-loop contributions: θ = (cid:0)I (cid:1) 1θΦ = (cid:0)J (cid:1)k θΦ, gB 1 (cid:0)J (cid:1)k θΦ. (B.2) k=0 k=0 Truncating to loops thus approximates the fixed-point gradient by the first terms of its Neumann series, whereas full BPTT uses the first . The extreme case = 1 keeps only the leading term θΦ; this is the one-step gradient used to train the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (Wang et al., 2025). When is contractive, the dropped terms shrink geometrically, which makes truncation plausible approximation at fraction of the backward compute. This idealized argument, however, does not settle whether truncation pays off in practice, for two reasons. First, it assumes that the loops reach fixed point, whereas looped language models are usually trained with only few loops (Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). With so few iterations, the states need not come close to fixed point, so the approximation Jt behind (B.2) can fail and the contributions dropped in (B.1) need not be small. Second, even at fixed point, the dropped terms are nonzero for < , so gB is biased estimate of the full gradient. The argument only bounds the error of single gradient, whereas this bias enters every update, and how it accumulates over training and shapes the final model is not known. Prior measurements compare recipes at fixed forward-loop count (2) and so cannot separate the compute that truncation saves from the loop gain it costs. We therefore measure the net effect directly: the scaling law of 4 asks whether the saved compute outweighs this bias in the loss that training actually reaches. Experimental setup Models We take the architecture and the training recipe of Schwethelm et al. (2026), the reference recipe below, which builds on the preluderecurrentcoda layout of Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) (3). Its blocks use pre-norm attention with querykey normalization and rotary position embeddings, head dimension 128, squared-ReLU feed-forward layer of width 4d, no biases, and untied input and output embeddings. We change only what is held fixed. Schwethelm et al. (2026) hold the executed depth fixed, so that more loops mean fewer unique layers; we hold the unique parameters fixed, as Prairie et al. (2026) do, so that loop setting changes the compute and not the model. The main grid spans five model sizes, from 58M to 919M non-embedding parameters  (Table 2)  ; width and depth grow together, and the recurrent block with the input injection holds 51% of the non-embedding parameters at four sizes and 56% at 120M. Short size names round ; including the untied input and output embeddings, total parameter counts run from about 107M to about 1.06B. We quote budgets per parameter as D/N . The scaling suite supplements this grid with two compute-matched pairs, adding the 79M and 162M models at one configuration each (E). Loop settings and budgets The scaling suite spans 1.11,291 training tokens per parameter and uses fifteen loop settings. Ten core settings, (1, 1); (2, 1) and (2, 2); (4, 1), (4, 2), (4, 3) and (4, 4); and (8, 2), (8, 4) and (8, 8), cover {1, 2, 4, 8} forward loops, full and truncated BPTT, and ratios B/T from 1 to 1. Five more settings extend them: (8, 1), and = 16 with = 1, 4, 8 and 16 4 at three sizes and short budgets (Appendices C.5 and G). The part of the training compute that depends on the loops grows with + 2B, since backward loop costs twice forward loop (D.1); (4, 1) thus costs as much per token as (2, 2), and (8, 2) as much as (4, 4). Token budgets are given in units of D0 = 230 1.07 109 tokens. We group runs by their target token budget; actual token counts may differ slightly because of batch rounding. Predictions use the actual token count D. An experimental configuration is choice of (N, D, T, B); run is one training execution of that configuration. Each configuration contributes one accepted validation loss to the analysis. Truncate or Not? Data and evaluation We train on the 100B-token sample of FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), the corpus of the looped scaling study of Lee et al. (2026), in pre-shuffled release,3 tokenized with the Llama 2 tokenizer (Touvron et al., 2023) of the reference recipe (Schwethelm et al., 2026) into sequences of 2,048 tokens. We report cross-entropy in nats per token on the last two shards of the release, which no run trains on, after removing the documents whose exact text also appears in the training data (the same web page often occurs in several crawls). Optimization We use the optimizers of the reference recipe (Schwethelm et al., 2026). MuonH, variant of Muon that keeps each weight matrix at fixed Frobenius norm (Jordan et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025), trains the hidden weight matrices (attention, feed-forward and input injection), and AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) trains the embedding, output and normalization parameters, both without weight decay. The MuonH update adds 0.065.7% to the compute of the forward and backward passes; the analysis leaves it out, and the measured compute we report includes it (D.1). The peak learning rates follow the references transfer rule (Ren et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2021), power law in the batch and training tokens with the token exponent re-estimated for our budgets, and the global batch grows as 64pD/D0 sequences, following the square-root scaling of the loss-optimal batch in prior work (Bergsma et al., 2025; Filatov et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b) (F). The learning rate warms up over the first 2% of steps and decays with cosine to 10% of its peak; gradients are not clipped. Runs and compute The results in this paper come from 592 training runs with 2.7 1022 FLOPs of training compute, counted as in D.1 with the optimizer update. The scaling suite contains 397 runs behind 347 configurations: 385 runs in the five-size grid (G) and 12 runs in two compute-matched pairs (E). Each configurations loss is the mean of its accepted runs. The remaining 195 distinct runs support the other experiments. These experiments comprise four more runs at 480M in Figure 13, nine further runs of the compute-optimal pairs and the 36 of the untied comparison (E), and the 66 learning-rate and 124 batch-size runs of Figures 17 and 18; 44 runs belong to two of these groups and are counted once. Counting cancelled runs, runs replaced by reruns, pilot runs and earlier calibration sweeps that the paper does not report, the study trained more than 1,100 runs with about 4.8 1022 FLOPs. The law in detail This appendix details the measured patterns behind the law, its fit and validation, the bounded gain, and the runs at sixteen loops. What the runs show before any law is fitted The measured losses separate the effects of forward and backward loops without fitted law (G). Forward loops that receive no gradient add almost nothing at first: at fixed B, doubling from to 2B changes the loss by less than 0.007 nats in all 24 sizebudget combinations trained in all ten core settings, while doubling it again, from 2B to 4B, lowers the loss in all 24. Spending the same compute per token on backward loops is better: (2, 2) beats (4, 1) and (4, 4) beats (8, 2) in all 24, by 0.023 nats on average for (2, 2) against (4, 1). Backward loops in turn have diminishing returns: with full BPTT, every doubling of = B, from 1 to 8, lowers the loss, by less each time, in all 24 combinations where all four settings were trained. 3https://huggingface.co/datasets/karpathy/fineweb-edu-100b-shuffle Truncate or Not? To estimate it from the runs, we first find the non-looped model size that matches looped runs measured loss at the same token budget. This defines the empirical effective size, which we then convert to looping coefficient using the runs parameter counts.
